projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Franklin James Klesack was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Franklin James Klesack. Mr. Klesack served in the US Navy onboard the aircraft carrier USS Wasp in the Pacific theater. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Klesack's home in Medina, Ohio on March 24th, 2004. Franklin was 83 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: 500 feet west. This is my dad's old farm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941, about?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: 21 or 22, something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, were you working at that time?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, on a farm. That was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of Pearl Harbor Day, December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, sure, I can remember that. I was working at Fairmont Creamery in Cleveland. I was coming home from work, and they announce it. And I listened to my radio on the car, and I listened to that on the radio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Terrible. That's what I thought. Everybody was buzzing on it. Nothing much you could do, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any thoughts of going out and signing up immediately for the service?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Not that day, but shortly thereafter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you did enlist then?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Early in '42?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Oh, go ahead if you need to get something}.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: -- yeah____+ Lloyd Ritz.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, so you enlisted with your neighbor?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah. So, okay. We went through boot camp, and through boot camp they divided us. And I went to the Wasp and he went to some other ship. And, about two years later -- about a year later -- I was down in Norfolk -- we was in Norfolk -- and I was on a streetcar. He gets on the streetcar. So I met him there. And then I was in the Pacific, on the Ana--Ana--Anatweak (ph) Island or something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, Anawetok?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Anawetok. I was on Anawetok. We was getting supplies. And I was standing up on the flight deck looking over. And here comes Lloyd Ritz with a little putter, delivering mail around the ship -- {laughs} -- so twice I met him. And one other guy I met -- he used to be a lifeguard down here at Hinckley Lake, and I knew him. And we was down to Trinidad and we had leave. I was swimming on this big beach and some guy was hollering my last name and I was looking all over; I couldn't figure out where the name was coming from. Finally, finally he says, "Hey, look up here, at the lifeguard stand!" There he was lifeguard down at Trinidad. So, that's two guys I met that I knew. So, it's a small world.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Getting back to training: When you first went into the Navy, was it tough being thrown in there with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not a tough adjustment?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No. I was young you know, you get to ____ just like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. What can you tell me about --

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: But there was guys that just couldn't handle it too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: That they discharged before they ever got through training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were some of the reasons they were discharged?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: I couldn't tell you, but they'd take 'em off to the doctor and all that, and the next thing you know they were gone, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: So, whether it was a ____ you know, could be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So, what can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: It was good. We had -- well, they give you all kind of exams and all that, to see whether you're mentally stable, I guess. But after nine weeks or twelve weeks, whatever it was, they said you can either go out now or you can go to school for six months and get a rating. So, I took the school and got third class when I got out of the school. I forget, I think it was four months. But, anyhow, they sent me on USS Santee -- down Norfolk, Virginia -- converted carrier, old converted carrier tanker. And these guys that were there -- I went over like a big lump, because here I am third class, and these guys been in the navy 14, 15 years, and they're still seamen. So, you know how that went over {laughs}. So anyhow, I was there. Never went out to sea on it. We's in port getting things all ready to go out, and this chief come up to me. He says, "You're goin' to the Wasp," he says, "we ain't foolin' with you anymore." So, I got a transfer to the Wasp. Boy, I was happy -- {laughs} go on, get out -- to get off of there. So, that's how I got on the Wasp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: I was a machinist mate, with steam and plumbing and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, when did you go on the Wasp then? Would that be--

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, and stayed on it until the war was over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you like the Wasp?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Good ship?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: It was a nice place to be, I thought. I always thought, pretty safe where I was. I was about 30 foot below sea level. And I thought I was pretty safe until we hit a SNAFU. A bomb came down through there and I didn't feel so safe after that {laughs}.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your first action on the Wasp?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, geez, I don't know. I can't remember but it was -- here you take a look.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'll take a look. This is a book on the history of the Wasp?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup. But here. You start out from the beginning.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you probably set sail sometime in '43 then, on the Wasp?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. What was life like on an aircraft carrier?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, it was pretty good. Always had something to eat, all that kind of stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, where -- when you first left the states -- where did you go? Obviously through the Panama Canal? Or tried to {laughs}.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, we went out to Pacific, that was the only place we was going for service in war action. And we traveled all over the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: First stop was Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, looks like from these pictures that you had some entertainment onboard ship? Can you tell me about that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Once in a while. I don't remember what it actually was, but, they'd have singers come on there, and dancers every once in a while. When we'd come in, like, into Hawaii or something like that. Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, describe any of the actions that you remember that you were involved in, in the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, the actions was mostly bombing. You know, they'd come down and try to get us. But, they missed most of the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These some kamikazes?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well that was, ____ like in 1945, end of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're talking about attacks from the Japanese Air Force?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, they'd come over and try to bomb us, and so forth, with their big Jap Betties, that which mounted like a B-24.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: And most the time they always got ____. I think there's pictures in there where they'll show you where they shoot them down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any close calls that you remember during those air raids?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, yeah. A lot of them. I think there's some pictures in there someplace.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. You involved in the invasion of the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Well, just go ahead and tell me anything you remember randomly, you know, it doesn't --

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, South Seas, China South Seas. We had -- looking for the Japanese fleet. Never did find it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. There's a sketch: "Randolph Hits at Movie Time".

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, I think it was Anawetok. I think that's where it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So there were --

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, you'd come into Anawetok and get reloaded -- you know, all those bombs and supplies and so forth -- and stay there few days and back out you went. And we's having a movie and that happened. They come over and threw a few bombs around.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, that was pretty close to you though?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, not close, but enough that we's moving {laughs}.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: According to the sketch in the book, they've got you guys watching a movie where a Navy gun is firing at the same time the Randolph was hit; was that true?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: {Laughing} -- Probably.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughing} -- You didn't know where the explosion was? Did you have any close buddies onboard ship?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, sure, whole bunch of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about them.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, I was in M division. M division had probably about 50 people in it. And M division is a engineering division down running the ship. And ____ I knew where they lived, you know, what they did, and so forth, before service and all that kind of stuff. So, it was kind of a close-knit group. So anyhow, with all the -- I went to one reunion here a couple years ago, and it was, like, one of the guys'd be there. And he died shortly after I come back home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Those are the only guys left from your division, you think?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: The only guys that were going to the reunion, and so forth, that kept contact. The rest of 'em were all gone, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies during the war?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup. We got bombed; quite a few of them were killed. And one guy, guy by the name of Frye -- he had a top bunk and there was an air conditioner going, blowing right on him. Everybody wanted that bunk, you know. But then he got killed, when the bomb hit; no one would take that bunk. {Laughs} -- Don't want it. So the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Superstitious?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh yeah. So, the bunk stayed empty for awhile before some new guy got -- come in and got replaced. {Laughs} -- Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there a lot of superstition onboard ship, things like that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just little things that caught your attention?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup. {Sound of pages turning} -- That's how we got hit, I think; there's a plane there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, exactly: "Bomb Hit on the Wasp". What's this down here? Well, that's a near miss; this is a picture of a near miss on the Hornet. And a picture of a bomb hit on the Wasp in March of '45. Do you remember that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a pretty bad one?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup. I was on the -- on the -- control panel down -- down -- in the engine room. And 52 gauges in front of me; and the gauges -- when we got hit -- the gauges were gone. Boom, boom -- all dropping. So anyhow, after the things dropped, a guy got on the phone and says, "Sailor, I want some steam! We gotta get out of here!" So anyhow, pretty quick, I says, "I can't do it. I haven't no steam on -- " I forget, seven and eight, something like that. I says, "I have nothing." Well, other guy comes on, "This is the captain speaking! Sailor, I want steam!" Well, I couldn't give it to them. Finally, it soaked in their head that boiler rooms were blew up, you know, went all the way down to the boiler room ____. So, we made five knots out of there. So, that's how we got away. So, that -- that was -- and then we went to Seattle. We got repaired. So, I forget -- what -- that was in April. And I think we went back out in July, maybe June, I forget. Took quite awhile to repair it because it was two boilers room blew up. And I was locked in the engine room. Well, we all were -- the guys that were on duty-- for, I think, 72 hours straight. And I passed us food through an escape hatch. So, it didn't bother me a bit, for some reason. Didn't make me nervous, nothing. I heard -- when the bomb went off -- I just heard "Whhff!" That was it. I felt a breeze, you know, that was about it. But the only problem was -- when the bomb did go off-- see they was -- they just blew all clear on quarters, and everything was open when it did happen. So, a lot of guys got killed, a 120-some I think. But that's in there someplace.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And was your -- the engine room -- sealed off because you had to keep it airtight? Just to --

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They sealed soon as you go down, they seal it from the top.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And they have to keep it locked because you were hit and they didn't want to --

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: They didn't know where the problem was until they all checked it all out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And this attack -- according to the pictures in this book -- this attack took place on March 19, 1945?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that the worst that -- when you were on the Wasp -- the worst damage you had?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: That's the worst damage.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you went back out in July where did you go? June or July?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: I think we was out around Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Japan, Okinawa, something like that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup, yup. You can see what it looked like.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, here's this. That's the hole in the hanger deck. And I forget how much steel was there, you know, maybe six, eight inches, whatever it was. And that bomb went through that like a .22 going through a piece of tin.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, this bomb went right on through and then exploded down in the boiler room?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Down in the boiler room.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, goodness.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup. That took out the chow hall and machine shop and I forget what else. Went right through it. Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you -- in '45 before this happened -- did you have any problem with kamikaze attacks?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They weren't in your area, huh?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No. After this -- after we went back out -- then we started getting kamikazes. 'Cause they figured they were getting kind of cornered.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that like? What did you feel like when you realized what the kamikazes were?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, just hoped they'd send up, oh man, what lead they'd send up. All you'd see, you know -- you had, what -- one out of three bullets' tracer. And all you could see was just all of them tracers going. Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And obviously part of that reason for the kamikazes was to frighten the men, you know; did it work at all?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Once in awhile. It was a ship hit. I think the Franklin got hit with a kamikaze.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah, exactly. The Franklin was the -- famous for -- or infamous, for a bad hit. Did you sail with the Franklin a lot?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Sometimes, I guess. It was in Task Force 58.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was Task Force 58, again?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: That was Halsey's Task Force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: In that you had a couple battleships. And I think there was four cans, and couple cruisers, and a couple aircraft carriers. And that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that the task force involved in the thing off the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where they went chasing --

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- something that wasn't there?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup. Yup. And then Halsey took us right into a hurricane. From all the stories I here nowadays, on the History Channel, he should have been court materialed -- marshalled -- or whatever you wanna call it {laughs}.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I believe I heard he took them into two different typhoons?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, could be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about going through that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Well, there's a picture in there that'll show you what happened {laughs}. Yeah, it busted down the flight deck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On the Wasp?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Geez.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: And we had to go to Pearl Harbor to get that fixed, before the planes could take off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, according to this picture, it says, "The Wasp Gets the Last Kamikaze of War".

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Must be, if it said so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Right there, there it is {laughs}.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: "Damaged Bow in Typhoon"; and this was in August, after VJ day.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that's the Wasp?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There's a picture of the Wasp and the flight deck is bent down almost, what, 45-degree angle?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: You can't believe the overhang, you know, on the flight deck. And those beams are about four-foot tall you know, about that tall. You know, it says the overhang of the deck comes out there, and those things are bent down just like pretzels.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did the task force lose a lot of ships during that typhoon?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: I think they lost three or four cans, and that was about it. The bigger ships were all right, but the destroyers -- they went down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Capsize 'em, huh?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, where were you on VJ day? Well, first of all, where were you on the day the bombs were dropped? The first bomb. Do you remember that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Someplace around Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing that news about the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you think of that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Didn't know what it was. So, one engineering officer, he explained it to us -- what an atomic bomb was. So, that's the first inkling I got of what an atomic bomb was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he had a pretty good idea of how it worked?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, sure. He knew the whole story, yup. So, I suppose being an engineer, you know, you get all that good stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly, if you read Popular Science or something at the time.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. So, do you remember any celebrations on VJ day when the war finally ended?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No, there wasn't much celebration, I don't remember, at any period.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did the Wasp go to Japan then after victory?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You came back -- what -- to back home?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: And then I was, this one engineering officer says to me, "Frank," he says, "so many guys are getting out, I wanna give you one grade up." He says, "If you sign in for six months -- a haul -- what we're gonna do is go over to Italy and haul soldiers back from Italy back to New York." Me, young, ____+ I don't want that. So, I got out. I wish I would have stayed because, the guys that did stay -- they sent me pictures and they were pretty darn nice. Yeah. Havin' a good time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, when did you finally get back home?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: In November, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: November of '45?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, I was discharged in Toledo, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: I guess they were happy, I don't know {laughs}.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}--I'm sure they were.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of mail call when you were onboard the Wasp?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, sure. They'd fire mail in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fire mail in?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Fly it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fly it? Oh, fly it.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Fly it, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: So, everybody used to wait for mail, no doubt about that. And it used to take, if I remember right, about a month, you know, to get. Which wasn't bad, you know. That's a lot of screwing around to get to you, yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get packages or anything like that from home?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Not very often because packages mean nothing like a ____+. Once I got some cigars and the worms got into them. And they were just pulverized, you know, just like a salad. {Rubbing hands together} -- Take 'em like this. So, that's where, you know, the heat and moisture, I guess, would do that. Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would they write to you?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: General things that were going on at home. Like, they were rationed for sugar and so much gasoline and so forth. Tell me all that kind of stuff, so, in other word, general news from home. {Laughs} -- Or gossip, whatever you want to call it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they think the rationing was a problem?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: It wasn't too much ____.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just something to talk about in the letters?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What would you write back to them?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Not much, 'cause everything was censored. You know, you couldn't say where you was, what you were doing, nothing. So, you just say hi and that's it. That was about it. Still alive and so forth. Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Oh, I haven't got -- no, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nothing that jumps out when you think about that time?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Nope. I was just happy to be alive, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: That's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's about it?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It says here: What historic person did you see? Did you see a historic person?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Mrs. Roosevelt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: When they christened the ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ahh.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: And John Jr. was on the ship until his dad died, and then I never saw him again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you talk to John?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Every payday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs} -- That was his job?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: That was his job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Sound of pages turning} -- And this was John Roosevelt?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah. There's the guys that died. Yeah, her picture should be here someplace. Here it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, that's -- you got a chance to see her?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: And there's John.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: And he went with us and stayed with us until -- 'til his dad died. And then I never saw him again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever talk to John about his dad?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No. All he did was paid me. He was the paymaster, we got 10 bucks a month.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 10 bucks a month?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yeah, if you got more than that, why, you were gambling with it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you remember anything else about when Eleanor christened the ship?

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You remember her being there.

sp.speaker: Franklin James Klesack
sp.p: Yup.
